subtype: Parking work by writing the next step [Response]
passage: Vijay, you can't sleep because your project is half done? Let me tell you what I learned in college, when I was a girl of nineteen. I was writing a long history essay, and at midnight I was only halfway. I shut my notebook and lay down, and the essay kept going round in my head. Which chapter next? Did I forget the dates? I didn't sleep a wink. The next night, same problem. So I tried something my roommate did. Before stopping, I wrote on a slip: "Start with the salt march paragraph, use page 42." I put the slip on top of my book. And I slept like a baby. My mind knew where to begin. That's your Urmila Nani's trick. Try it.

qa.q: What page did Urmila note on the slip?
qa.a: Page 42.

qa.q: How did young Urmila feel the first night she stopped halfway?
qa.a: Urmila felt restless and anxious, the unfinished essay going round and round, so sleep wouldn't come.

qa.q: What choice in the story solved the problem?
qa.a: Writing exactly where to start next on a slip before stopping, which let her mind rest.

qa.q: How might Vijay feel after hearing the story?
qa.a: Vijay might feel relieved and hopeful, with a simple trick to try for his own half-done project.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how, as a college student, writing down the next step let her rest despite unfinished work.

passage: Note to self, Friday, after dinner with Rajni. I'm Elizabeth, and Rajni has been my closest friend at the firm for two years. Tonight she barely touched her biryani. She checked her phone every few minutes, started sentences and forgot the ends. "Sorry, I keep thinking about the budget sheet. And the vendor email. And the slides." None of them were finished. She said she'd been sleeping badly for a week. I didn't lecture. I tore a page from my diary and said, "Tell me everything that's half done." We wrote seven things. Next to each, she wrote a day and time. By the time dessert came, she was laughing again. What I'll do next: check in on Monday to see if the list helped.

qa.q: How many half-done things did Rajni and Elizabeth write down?
qa.a: Seven things.

qa.q: What might Rajni have been feeling during dinner?
qa.a: Rajni seemed distracted and anxious, her mind stuck on unfinished tasks, and tired from poor sleep.

qa.q: Why did writing the list with times help Rajni?
qa.a: Scheduling each open task gave her mind a place to park them, so they stopped pulling at her attention.

qa.q: What seems to be on Elizabeth's mind as she writes this note?
qa.a: Elizabeth seems caring and a little concerned about Rajni, and hopeful the list will help.

grounding: Illustrates a colleague noticing a friend distracted by open tasks and suggesting listing and scheduling them.

passage: On Lohri night, after too many peanuts and rewri, Preeti curled up on the sofa. "My tummy hurts." Her big brother Ujjwal sat beside her and rubbed her back. Papa came from the kitchen with a tiny white mishri sweet. "Here. This will help settle it." Preeti sucked it slowly while Papa put a warm cloth on her tummy and told her about the bonfire songs. "Better?" he asked after a while. "A bit," she said, and it was true. The ache had softened. "If it keeps hurting or you feel worse, tell me, and we'll call the doctor," Papa said. Ujjwal whispered, "That's just sugar." Papa smiled. "Sugar and care."

qa.q: What did Papa give Preeti?
qa.a: A tiny white mishri sweet.

qa.q: How did Preeti feel after Papa's sweet and the warm cloth?
qa.a: She felt comforted and a little better, as the ache softened with Papa's care and reassurance.

qa.q: What did Papa do wisely besides giving the sweet?
qa.a: He stayed with her, used a warm cloth, and said they would call the doctor if it kept hurting or she felt worse.

qa.q: How does Ujjwal see the mishri?
qa.a: Ujjwal thinks it's "just sugar" and doesn't realise how much the reassurance itself helps.

grounding: Shows a child's stomach ache easing after a caring parent gives a harmless sweet and says it will help.

passage: The monsoon had made the canteen floor muddy. "Don't eat the rajma," Sangeeta whispered as they queued. "Why?" asked Nandini. "A girl in 10B said it made half her class sick last week." "Seriously?" Nandini looked at her plate. Suddenly the smell seemed off. "I feel a bit sick already." "You haven't even eaten it!" "I know, but my stomach's turning." She pushed the plate away. "Did anyone actually get sick?" Sangeeta shrugged. "That's what she said." The canteen uncle overheard. "Beta, the health inspector came yesterday. All fine." Nandini took a small bite, cautiously. The queasy feeling slowly faded. "Weird," she said. "I really felt it."

qa.q: What dish did Sangeeta warn Nandini about?
qa.a: The rajma.

qa.q: Why did Nandini feel sick before eating?
qa.a: She felt anxious after hearing the rumour, and that worry made her stomach turn as if the food were already making her ill.

qa.q: What could Nandini do next time she hears a rumour like this?
qa.a: Check the facts first, as the canteen uncle's news helped, before letting worry decide how she feels.

qa.q: How might the canteen uncle feel overhearing the girls?
qa.a: He might feel a bit hurt or worried that a rumour is spreading about food he knows is fine.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager feeling nauseous from an anxious expectation before eating, the nocebo effect.

passage: Last winter, in exam season, the doctor gave me allergy tablets, and I, Avni, did the worst possible thing: I read the whole leaflet, every tiny line. Headache. Dizziness. Dry mouth. Tiredness. That night, I felt all of them. Every twinge was on the list. My friend Lalit came to study and found me lying on the floor, sure something awful was happening. He read the leaflet and said, "These say 'rare'. And you've got exams, you'd be tired anyway." That calmed me. But a headache kept coming back for days, so I didn't just ignore it. I called the doctor and told her about it and my worries. She went through it with me and changed the tablet. Fear made most of it bigger, but not all.

qa.q: What kind of tablets did the doctor give Avni?
qa.a: Allergy tablets.

qa.q: How did Avni feel after reading the leaflet?
qa.a: Avni felt frightened and anxious, noticing every twinge as one of the listed effects.

qa.q: What did Avni do right about the headache that kept coming back?
qa.a: Instead of ignoring it or panicking, Avni called the doctor, shared the worries, and let the doctor decide what to change.

qa.q: How does Lalit help Avni?
qa.a: Lalit reads the leaflet calmly, points out the effects are rare and that exams cause tiredness, which settles Avni's fear.

grounding: Shows a young adult noticing twinges as listed side effects out of fear, while still taking a persistent symptom to the doctor.

passage: I'm Sunaina, a junior nurse on the children's ward, and last week I learned something no textbook said clearly. A little boy came in with a cut on his arm that needed cleaning. His mother was frantic, hovering, saying, "Oh no, oh no, it's going to hurt so much." He screamed before anyone touched him. Then Lakshmi, our senior nurse, knelt down. Her voice was slow and warm. "I'm going to clean this. It'll sting a little, and then it's done. Can you count the fish on my badge?" He counted. He winced, but he didn't scream. His mother watched, and her shoulders dropped. I realised the way Lakshmi spoke wasn't extra to the care. It was part of the care.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi ask the boy to count?
qa.a: The fish on her badge.

qa.q: What did Sunaina realise while watching Lakshmi?
qa.a: Sunaina felt surprised and impressed, realising that a calm voice is part of the care itself, not an extra.

qa.q: What could Sunaina copy from Lakshmi when caring for a scared child?
qa.a: Speaking slowly and warmly, saying honestly what will happen, and giving the child something to focus on, like counting.

qa.q: How might the boy's mother have felt after watching Lakshmi?
qa.a: The mother seemed to calm down, her shoulders dropping, perhaps relieved and a little aware of how her panic had affected him.

grounding: Illustrates a young nurse observing that a calm, confident voice settles a child in pain while anxious hovering worsens it.

passage: Before my small knee operation last spring, I, Bhupen, decided to be hopeful. My wife Leela and I talked about the trek we'd do once I healed, and that helped. But I didn't pretend I wasn't scared. I told the surgeon, "I'm worried about the anaesthesia," and asked what usually happens and what doesn't. She explained both sides plainly. That made the fear smaller. After the operation, I kept hopeful. But when a pain on the side of the knee didn't settle, I didn't tell myself it was in my head. Leela said, "Call them." I did. It turned out to need a small adjustment to my exercises. Hope helped me heal. It didn't replace checking.

qa.q: What did Bhupen and Leela plan to do once he healed?
qa.a: A trek.

qa.q: How did Bhupen feel before the operation, and what helped?
qa.a: He felt hopeful but also scared about the anaesthesia; telling the surgeon and hearing both sides plainly made the fear smaller.

qa.q: What did Bhupen do wisely when the pain didn't settle?
qa.a: He didn't dismiss it as imagination; he called the doctors, who adjusted his exercises.

qa.q: How does Leela support Bhupen?
qa.a: Leela shares his hopeful plans but also pushes him to call when the pain doesn't settle.

grounding: Shows an adult using hopeful expectation while still telling the doctor his worries and not dismissing a lasting symptom.

passage: Before: In Diwali week, the nursery teacher held up Vishal's diya drawing. "Vishal is so bright!" She gave him an extra smile and waited while he explained his colours. During: The next week, she asked Vishal the hard counting questions and said, "Take your time, you can do it." He tried longer than before. Raghav, beside him, got an easier question, quickly. After: By the end of the month, Vishal was the first to put up his hand, even when he wasn't sure. "I'm bright," he told his Nani.

qa.q: What did Vishal draw in Diwali week?
qa.a: A diya.

qa.q: Why did Vishal start putting his hand up even when unsure?
qa.a: He felt confident and encouraged, because the teacher treated him as bright and gave him time.

qa.q: How could the teacher give Raghav the same chance?
qa.a: She could give Raghav hard questions too, wait for him, and say "you can do it."

qa.q: How might Raghav feel getting easier questions quickly?
qa.a: Raghav might feel less important and start trying less, noticing that Vishal gets more time and smiles.

grounding: Illustrates a young child called bright receiving more time and encouragement and beginning to act bright.

subtype: Labelled weak and living down to it [Receiver]
passage: Harvest season in the village school meant half-empty benches and a tired teacher. From the first term, Master had called Sonali "weak in maths." He said it kindly, but it stuck. Now, when he asked questions, he looked straight past her to Harsha, and waited a long time for Harsha to answer. If Sonali raised her hand, he'd say, "Let someone else try." So she stopped raising it. She stopped trying the extra sums too. What was the point? In the monthly test, she left half the page blank. Master sighed. "As I thought." Sonali stared at the blank half. She had known two of those answers. Nobody had ever waited long enough to find out.

qa.q: Who did Master wait a long time for?
qa.a: Harsha.

qa.q: What was Sonali feeling as she stared at the blank half of the page?
qa.a: She felt discouraged and a little bitter, knowing she had some answers but had stopped trying because nobody expected her to.

qa.q: What could Master do differently to give Sonali a fair chance?
qa.a: Wait as long for Sonali's answers as for Harsha's and ask her real questions, instead of saying "let someone else try".

qa.q: How might Harsha be affected by Master's attention?
qa.a: Harsha probably feels capable and keeps trying, since Master expects answers and waits for them.

grounding: Shows a child labelled weak at maths receiving fewer chances and less waiting time, until the label comes true.

subtype: Family verdict about who they will become [Receiver]
passage: You want to know why I get quiet at Diwali, Didi? Every year, at Nani's house, some aunty says, "Sarika, you'll never be like your cousin Rajni." Rajni the topper. Rajni the doctor-to-be. At first I laughed. Then I started believing it. Why study hard if I'll never be Rajni anyway? My marks dropped. I stopped trying for the science stream. But this Diwali, after the aunties said it again, Papa came up to the terrace where I was hiding. He didn't compare. He just said, "I've watched you fix that radio for two weeks. You keep going. That's the thing I believe in." I don't know. It's small. But I've started staying back for the physics practicals again.

qa.q: Where was Sarika hiding when Papa came to talk?
qa.a: On the terrace.

qa.q: How did the aunties' words make Sarika feel over the years?
qa.a: Sarika felt discouraged and small, slowly believing there was no point trying because Sarika would never match Rajni.

qa.q: What did Papa say that helped, and why?
qa.a: He praised Sarika's persistence in fixing the radio, showing belief in effort rather than comparing with Rajni.

qa.q: How might Rajni feel if she knew about the aunties' comparisons?
qa.a: Rajni might feel uncomfortable being used as a measuring stick against her cousin.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager absorbing a family verdict about who she will become, and a parent's belief in effort quietly lifting the teen.
